items: Bago City launched a children's book titled 'Ang Kanyon ni Juan' to educate young readers about General Juan Anacleto Araneta, a 19th-century revolutionary hero, addressing both a generation gap and literacy issues.
The book, written in Hiligaynon with simple dialogue and illustrations, aims to make the story accessible to young children, with plans for mass production following its launch.

The initiative is part of a broader effort to improve literacy rates in Bago, where many students are identified as frustrated readers, and the mayor envisions a series of books to continue this educational mission.

NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines – It takes just 32 glossy pages, simple Hiligaynon dialogue, and bright illustrations to reintroduce a 19th-century revolutionary hero to a young child.

Launched on November 5 alongside the 128th anniversary of Negros Occidental’s bloodless revolution, Al Cinco de Noviembre, Bago City’s new children’s book — Ang Kanyon ni Juan (The Cannon of Juan) — hopes to address the growing generation gap and the struggles of young readers.

For Bago Mayor Mayette Javellana-Yao, the problem was impossible to ignore. Most of the city’s younger generation, she candidly admitted, do not really know who the late General Juan Anacleto Araneta (Tan Juan) is — one of the two heroes who put Negros Occidental on the map of Philippine history by leading a bloodless uprising against Spanish colonizers on November 5, 1898.

At the same time, literacy numbers weighed heavily on her mind. The 2025–2026 End-of-School-Year Reading Profile for Grades 4 to 10 in English and Filipino, alongside the Comprehensive Literacy Assessment for Grades 1 to 3, revealed a troubling picture.
Using the Philippine Informal Reading Inventory (Phil-IRI) methodology, assessments showed that the city still has many frustrated readers.

To tackle both challenges at once, the city government teamed up early this year with the Department of Education (DepEd) Schools Division of Bago and the Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) Federation to bring Tan Juan’s story to life for young readers.

The mayor requested that the book be written in Hiligaynon, featuring simple paragraphs and an accessible layout so that even a five-year-old child can easily grasp its message. Each 8×8-inch page pairs a large illustration of the characters with a four-paragraph dialogue centered on Tan Juan.
Bringing the pages to life were two creatives from DepEd-Bago: education program specialist II Roxan “Dondon” del Castillo as author, and art teacher Jullienne Castillo as illustrator.
For Del Castillo, the project was deeply personal — he is a fourth-generation descendant of Tan Juan’s clan.
Meanwhile, the SK Federation of Bago spearheaded the printing. Fifty copies were presented to guests during the launch, with mass production set to follow soon, the mayor said.

For Javellana-Yao, seeing the book come to fruition was the fulfillment of a dream years in the making. “Actually, I have envisioned this book since I entered politics in 2018 as a councilor,” she confided.
“Really,” the mayor said, “it pains me to hear and see children passing by the monument of Tan Juan in front of the Bago City Coliseum saying, ‘Who is he?'”

A former campus journalist at St. John’s Institute in Bacolod City during high school and at the University of the Philippines Visayas in Miag-ao, Iloilo during college, Javellana-Yao had long felt an inner drive to publish a book about Tan Juan once she had the means to do so. When she was elected mayor in May 2025 and took office in July, making that book a reality became one of her top priorities.
Sixteen months into her term, that vision finally took shape — born out of a practical question she had asked herself for years.

“I always ask myself, if the city government is spending so much every November 5 to commemorate Al Cinco de Noviembre, why can’t we publish a book — a series, at that — that will last forever?” Javellana-Yao said.
And after 128 years, this marks the first time Al Cinco de Noviembre and Tan Juan have a book published right here in Bago — not bulky, yet truly educational and inspirational, she added.

The urgency behind the project is underscored by Bago’s recent Phil-IRI End-of-School-Year Reading Profile results. The neophyte mayor said she was disturbed to learn that from Grades 4 to 10, many students across the city remain frustrated readers:
A similar picture emerged from the 2025–2026 End-of-School-Year Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment for Grades 1 to 3, which evaluated 8,551 students:

items: 33.60% (2,874 students) are reading at grade level

blocks.text: Faced with these numbers, the mayor is convinced that early intervention is critical — and that a simple storybook could help turn the tide.

“That’s why I want the book to be simple and written in Hiligaynon, so it can be easily understood by students at the day care and kindergarten levels,” the mayor explained. Once children learn to read starting in day care through their mother tongue, she stressed, they can build a lasting reading habit and smoothly advance to higher grades.
Ang Kanyon ni Juan is only the beginning. According to Javellana-Yao, five more sequels are planned, starting with Requinto: Ang Kabayo ni Tan Juan, which is already in the pipeline.

To help sustain the series and defray printing costs, senior tourism supervising officer Mae Ann Furtos said the city will also coordinate with the National Historical Commission of the Philippines (NHCP) to see if the book qualifies for publishing grants. – Rappler.com
